periods.activity_title: Weighing Before and After — Does Mass Change in Physical Changes
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing a balance with beaker before and after dissolution

time_bands.activity: Pose the opening question: when water forms from hydrogen and oxygen, is the total mass the same as the sum of the parts? Students briefly discuss in pairs, predicting whether mass changes during physical changes.

Students carry out Activity 9.1: weigh an empty beaker, add approximately 50 mL of water and record the mass, add a spatula of common salt, stir until dissolved, and record the mass again. Groups compare their before-and-after readings.
Class collates results on the board. Students explain in writing why the reading did not change, framing their answer around the idea that dissolving rearranges particles without destroying any.
Teacher draws the connection to the formal statement of the Law of Conservation of Mass (Lavoisier, 1789). Students rewrite the law in their own words and note it in their science journals.

periods.teacher_notes: This is the chapter's entry point, so begin by surfacing what students already think about mass and change — many assume that dissolving destroys some material. Watch for the misconception that a substance 'disappears' when dissolved; the stable balance reading directly contradicts this. Ask groups whose readings show a tiny change to consider sources of experimental error rather than concluding mass was not conserved.
homework: A candle burns and the wax appears to decrease. Using the Law of Conservation of Mass, explain where the mass goes — write two or three sentences identifying all products of the reaction.

periods.activity_title: Open vs Closed Systems — Testing Mass Conservation in Chemical Changes
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram of Set-up 1 (balloon beside flask) and Set-up 2 (balloon fixed to flask mouth)

time_bands.activity: Pose the inquiry question: if a chemical reaction produces a gas that escapes, does the measured mass decrease? Students predict outcomes for an open and a closed system before seeing any results.

Groups run Activity 9.2 in both set-ups — Set-up 1 with the balloon containing baking soda placed beside the flask (open), and Set-up 2 with the balloon fitted to the flask mouth (closed). They record initial and final masses for each and compare.
Class compares the two sets of readings. Students reason in writing: the lower final mass in Set-up 1 is because the carbon dioxide escaped the system, not because mass was destroyed.
Teacher works through the two numerical examples from Section 9.1 on the board — calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid, and carbon burning — having students supply the arithmetic at each step.

periods.teacher_notes: The most important misconception to address is that the lower mass in the open set-up means mass was destroyed; redirect students to the escaped carbon dioxide as the 'missing' mass still present in the room. Having established through Activity 9.1 that mass is conserved in physical changes, this unit asks whether the same holds when new substances form. A good checkpoint is whether students can articulate why closing the system is essential before they move on to the numerical examples.

periods.activity_title: Precipitation and Proportions — Verifying and Applying Mass Conservation
materials: Two small beakers or test tubes

time_bands.activity: Students set up Activity 9.3: weigh two beakers each containing one of the solutions, then mix them, observe the white precipitate of barium sulfate forming, and reweigh. They record and compare initial total mass with final mass.

Class confirms that even when a precipitate forms — a new solid substance — the total mass is unchanged. Students write a one-paragraph argument explaining why this is consistent with Lavoisier's law.

Think as a Scientist task: students design their own experiment using zinc and dilute hydrochloric acid to test mass conservation. They sketch their set-up, list the measurements they would take, and predict what result would confirm or refute the law.

Groups share designs. Teacher leads a brief class discussion on which set-ups would capture the hydrogen gas produced and which would not, connecting back to the closed-system lesson from Activity 9.2.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students who believe a precipitate represents 'new' mass appearing; the Activity 9.3 data shows the precipitate's mass comes entirely from the dissolved ions already in solution. The design task builds on the closed-system reasoning students developed in Activity 9.2, and the zinc-acid system provides a clean analogue — hydrogen gas plays the same role carbon dioxide did. Push students to specify exactly which apparatus choice ensures the gas is not lost.

periods.activity_title: Fixed Ratios Always — Exploring the Law of Constant Proportions
periods.visual_aids: Board table showing water decomposition data from river, borewell, and ocean sources with consistent 1:8 hydrogen:oxygen ratio

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the question: if water is collected from three different sources and decomposed, will the ratio of hydrogen to oxygen always be the same? Students vote on their prediction before any data is shown.

Teacher explains Proust's Law with the water example (1:8 by mass), then works through the sodium chloride example (23:35.5 ratio) on the board, showing how to use the ratio to find how much chlorine reacts with 46 g of sodium.

Students read the Threads of Curiosity inset about cinnabar (hingula) and calculate: given the 86.22% Hg and 13.78% S mass percentages, how many grams of sulfur would be found in 100 g of cinnabar processed anywhere in the world? They compare answers in pairs.

Teacher draws out the key distinction: the law is about the ratio by mass, not the amount of the compound. Students write a two-sentence summary distinguishing this law from the Law of Conservation of Mass.

periods.teacher_notes: A very common confusion is between 'same ratio by mass' and 'same total amount' — students may think that different sources of water give different amounts, not just different absolute masses of hydrogen and oxygen. The cinnabar example is powerful because it is cross-cultural and historical, showing the law holds regardless of who performs the decomposition. Ask students: does the law say anything about how much cinnabar you start with, or only about the ratio?
homework: A sample of ammonia is found to contain nitrogen and hydrogen in a mass ratio of 14:3. If a different sample of ammonia weighs 34 g, calculate the mass of nitrogen and the mass of hydrogen it contains, showing your working.

periods.activity_title: Atoms as Explanation — Reasoning Through Dalton's Postulates
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram: hydrogen + oxygen → water, with circles labelled H and O showing rearrangement, not creation or destruction

time_bands.activity: Teacher revisits the two laws students have established — conservation of mass and constant proportions — and poses the question: what particle-level picture would explain both laws at once? Students brainstorm in pairs and write their ideas on sticky notes.
Teacher introduces Dalton's six postulates one at a time. For each postulate, students identify which law (or both) it explains and place a sticky note on the corresponding column on the board.

Students work on the 'What if…' reflective task: if atoms could combine in any ratio rather than fixed whole-number ratios, what would happen to the identity and predictability of substances? They write a short paragraph and share with a partner.

Class debrief: teacher asks students which postulate does the heaviest lifting in explaining the Law of Constant Proportions, and which explains conservation of mass. Students record the conclusion in their journals.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often memorise the postulates without understanding which law each one explains; the sticky-note mapping makes the logical connection visible and assessable. Watch for the misconception that atoms are created during reactions — the magnesium burning example (magnesium atoms and oxygen atoms rearranging to form magnesium oxide) is the cleanest rebuttal. The 'What if…' prompt works best when students are pressed to name a concrete substance that would lose its identity if ratios were variable.

periods.activity_title: Why Atoms Bond — Stability, Molecules, and the Two Broad Pathways
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram: valence-shell diagrams for He (stable, 2 electrons) vs H (1 electron, needs one more) and Cl (7 electrons, needs one more), with arrows labelled 'share' and 'transfer'

time_bands.activity: Teacher recalls the valence-shell structure from Chapter 8 — atoms are stable when the outermost shell has eight electrons (or two if the K-shell is outermost) — and asks: what does an atom with only one or two valence electrons 'want' to do? Students predict strategies.

Teacher explains the definition of a molecule, the special stability of noble gases like helium, and the principle that bonding lowers the total energy of the system. The two bonding pathways — sharing (covalent) and transfer (ionic) — are introduced as names only, with examples deferred.

Students sort four given atoms — H, Cl, Na, O — by their valence electron counts and predict, using the 'fewer than four donate, more than four gain or share' rule, which strategy each would likely use. They record predictions in their notebooks.

Class shares predictions. Teacher confirms or corrects each, setting up the concrete bond-formation examples that follow in subsequent units. Students write a one-sentence definition of a chemical bond in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'stability' with 'inactivity'; emphasise that stability here means reaching the noble-gas electron configuration, not that the atom stops doing anything. Having revisited the octet and duplet rules from Chapter 8, this unit frames both bonding types as solutions to the same problem — incomplete valence shells. The sorting task works well as a quick pair activity and surfaces any lingering confusion about valence electron counts before the detailed bond-formation units begin.

periods.activity_title: Sharing Electrons — Covalent Bonds in Elemental Molecules H₂, Cl₂, and O₂
periods.section_anchor: 9.4.1 Bonding by sharing of electrons — Covalent Bond
periods.visual_aids: Board electron-dot diagrams for H₂ (single bond), Cl₂ (single bond with lone pairs), and O₂ (double bond), showing shared and unshared electrons

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws the electron configuration of a single hydrogen atom (1 electron in K-shell) and asks: if two hydrogen atoms come close together, how could they both achieve a full K-shell without any electron leaving either atom? Students propose the sharing idea before it is named.

Teacher works through the formation of H₂ (single bond), Cl₂ (single bond, with seven valence electrons each), and O₂ (double bond, six valence electrons each) using electron-dot diagrams, connecting the number of electrons short to the number of bonds formed.

Students practise independently: for each of the three molecules, they draw the electron-dot diagram, count shared and unshared electron pairs, and write the structural formula (H—H, Cl—Cl, O=O). They check each other's diagrams in pairs.

Teacher draws the pattern on the board: 'electrons short' → 'bonds formed'. Students articulate the rule in one sentence and note whether H₂ and Cl₂ form the same bond type despite different atomic sizes.

periods.teacher_notes: The central misconception to address is that a shared electron 'belongs' to one atom; emphasise that both atoms simultaneously count it toward their octet. Students often struggle with oxygen's double bond — prompt them to count how many electrons oxygen needs and how many a single bond would provide, so the double bond emerges from necessity rather than memorisation. Electron-dot diagram accuracy is the key checkpoint before moving to compound molecules.

periods.activity_title: Covalent Bonds in Compounds — HCl, H₂O, and Naming Covalent Substances
periods.section_anchor: 9.4.1 Bonding by sharing of electrons — Covalent Bond
periods.visual_aids: Board table of prefix names (mono- through hexa-) alongside worked naming examples CO, CO₂, N₂O₄

time_bands.activity: Teacher works through covalent bond formation in HCl (hydrogen needs one electron, chlorine needs one — single bond) and H₂O (oxygen needs two, each hydrogen contributes one — two single bonds to the same oxygen), using electron-dot diagrams on the board.

Teacher introduces the prefix naming system for covalent compounds, covering mono- through hexa-, the vowel-dropping rule, and the special rule for hydrogen as the first element (no prefix). Students copy the prefix table and apply it to CO, CO₂, CS₂, and PCl₃.

Students work in pairs to name SF₆, N₂O₄, and N₂O₅, and then reverse the task — given 'dinitrogen pentoxide', they write the formula. They also note H₂O (water) and NH₃ (ammonia) as common-name exceptions.
Brief class check: teacher reads out four formulae and students write names on mini-whiteboards or paper, held up simultaneously so the teacher can scan for errors before moving on.

periods.teacher_notes: Watch for students adding 'mono-' to the first element — the rule that mono- is omitted for the first element is frequently overlooked, so drilling it with CO vs. carbon monoxide is worthwhile. Having built up electron-dot diagrams for elemental covalent molecules, this unit extends the same logic to compounds and then layers on the naming convention, which is purely definitional. The mini-whiteboard check at the close gives a quick read on whether the naming rules have been internalised before the ionic bond unit begins.
homework: Name each of the following covalent compounds and write the structural formula showing the bonds: (a) HBr, (b) CCl₄, (c) N₂O. Show your working for the prefix choices.

periods.activity_title: Electron Transfer and Ion Formation — Building the Ionic Bond in NaCl
periods.section_anchor: 9.4.2 Bonding by electron transfer — Ionic bond
periods.visual_aids: Board step-by-step diagram: Na (2,8,1) loses one electron → Na⁺ (2,8); Cl (2,8,7) gains one electron → Cl⁻ (2,8,8); electrostatic attraction shown between ions

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks: sodium has only one valence electron — sharing one electron with another atom would give sodium 2, but it needs 8. What alternative strategy is available? Students propose 'give it away' before the transfer mechanism is named.

Teacher works through the formation of NaCl step by step: Na loses its single valence electron (becomes Na⁺ with 11 protons, 10 electrons), Cl gains it (becomes Cl⁻ with 17 protons, 18 electrons), and the resulting opposite charges attract. Students draw each step alongside the teacher.

Teacher introduces the crystal lattice structure from the Threads of Curiosity inset — each Na⁺ surrounded by six Cl⁻ and vice versa — contrasting this with the discrete molecules formed by covalent bonding. Students sketch the 3-D arrangement as described.

Students write the names of three given ionic compounds (NaCl, MgCl₂, CaO) using the cation-then-anion naming rule, and identify whether each ion is mono- or polyatomic, referencing Table 9.1 in the textbook.

periods.teacher_notes: The most persistent misconception here is that ions are unstable or temporary — emphasise that Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are fully stable species with complete outer shells. Students sometimes apply the covalent-bond logic and think NaCl has 'shared' electrons; the step-by-step proton-count diagram (11 protons vs 10 electrons for Na⁺) makes the transfer concrete. The crystal lattice point is important because it distinguishes ionic compounds from covalent molecules structurally, which pays off directly in the properties comparison unit.

periods.activity_title: Naming Ions and Ionic Compounds — Mono- and Polyatomic Ion Tables
periods.section_anchor: 9.4.2 Bonding by electron transfer — Ionic bond
materials: Flashcard sets (ion name, formula, charge — prepared by students in the first phase)
periods.visual_aids: Projected or board copy of Table 9.1 — monoatomic and polyatomic ions with formulae and valencies

time_bands.activity: Students study Table 9.1 in pairs. Each pair creates a set of mini-flashcards (index-card scraps or notebook paper): ion name on one side, formula and charge on the other. They focus first on the monoatomic ions, grouping by charge (1+, 2+, 3+, 1−, 2−).

Pairs quiz each other using the flashcards. Teacher circulates, probing with questions: 'Why does iron appear twice in this table?' and 'How does the name of a polyatomic ion differ from that of a monoatomic anion?'

Teacher dictates six ionic compound combinations (e.g. Ca²⁺ + Cl⁻, Fe³⁺ + O²⁻, NH₄⁺ + SO₄²⁻). Students write the name of each compound using the cation-first rule and note whether any involve polyatomic ions.
Class debriefs: teacher draws out the pattern that polyatomic ions do not end in -ide, and that naming the compound does not change the ion names. Students add this rule to their notes.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse the charge on an ion with its valency; making the flashcards helps them build the ion as a whole unit (name + formula + charge) rather than memorising columns separately. Iron appearing as both Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺ is a common source of confusion — ask students to find another element in the table with two oxidation states and discuss why this happens at a surface level. The six dictated combinations should include at least one polyatomic anion and one NH₄⁺ so both ion types are practiced.
homework: Using Table 9.1 from Section 9.4.2, write the correct name for each of these ionic compounds: (a) K₂S, (b) AlCl₃, (c) Ca(OH)₂, (d) (NH₄)₂CO₃. For each, identify whether the anion is monoatomic or polyatomic.

periods.activity_title: Criss-Cross in Action — Writing Formulae of Covalent Compounds
periods.visual_aids: Board worked example of criss-cross steps for HCl, H₂S, and CCl₄ — symbols, valencies below, arrows crossing, subscript result

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the criss-cross method as a shortcut: write the element symbols, write their valencies below, criss-cross the valencies as subscripts, and drop any subscript of one. Demonstrates with HCl (1,1 → HCl) and H₂S (1,2 → H₂S) on the board.

Teacher works through CCl₄ (4,1 → CCl₄), then asks students to predict the formula for PH₃ before showing the working. Students practise four more covalent pairs from the textbook independently, writing each step explicitly.

Peer-check: students swap notebooks and check each other's criss-cross steps, flagging any case where the subscript of 1 was written rather than omitted. Teacher circulates and addresses systematic errors.

Teacher poses the reverse task: given the formula SiCl₄, students identify the valencies used and verify they are consistent with the expected valencies for silicon (4) and chlorine (1). Class discusses whether the criss-cross always gives the simplest ratio for covalent compounds.

periods.teacher_notes: The most common procedural error is forgetting to omit the subscript 1, leading to formulae like H₁Cl₁ rather than HCl; the peer-check step targets exactly this. Students coming from the ionic bond unit need to be clear that the criss-cross method in this sub-section applies to covalent compounds and uses valency, not ionic charge — that distinction will matter immediately. The reverse task (SiCl₄ → valencies) is a good checkpoint for whether students understand what the subscripts represent.

periods.activity_title: Criss-Cross for Ionic Compounds — Charges, Brackets, and Simplest Ratios
periods.visual_aids: Board worked examples of CaCl₂, Al₂O₃, MgO, CaCO₃, Mg(OH)₂, Al₂(SO₄)₃ showing all criss-cross steps including bracket placement

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the additional steps for ionic compounds: write the cation first, write charges beneath (not as superscripts), criss-cross only the numbers, then simplify by dividing by the highest common factor. Works through CaCl₂ and Al₂O₃ fully on the board.

Teacher demonstrates MgO (equal valencies simplify to 1:1), then CaCO₃ and Mg(OH)₂, emphasising that brackets are used when a polyatomic ion appears more than once and that the charge on the ion is NOT shown in the final formula.
Students work through Al(OH)₃ and Al₂(SO₄)₃ independently, showing all criss-cross steps. They identify where brackets are needed and where the simplest ratio requires division.

Class correction on the board: teacher works through Al₂(SO₄)₃ step by step, calling on students to supply each step. Common errors — brackets omitted, charges retained in final formula — are highlighted.

periods.teacher_notes: Retaining the ionic charge in the final formula (writing Ca²⁺Cl₂⁻ rather than CaCl₂) is the most common error, and it is worth stating the rule explicitly: charges are not shown in the compound formula. Students who correctly simplified MgO to 1:1 sometimes doubt themselves; confirm that the criss-cross giving Mg₂O₂ must be divided by 2. The bracket rule is the key new element here — remind students that brackets signal a polyatomic ion being multiplied, not just grouping for appearance.
homework: Write the chemical formulae for the following ionic compounds using the criss-cross method, showing all working: (a) potassium sulfide (K⁺, S²⁻), (b) iron(III) chloride (Fe³⁺, Cl⁻), (c) barium nitrate (Ba²⁺, NO₃⁻), (d) zinc hydroxide (Zn²⁺, OH⁻).

periods.activity_title: Solubility and Conductivity — Comparing Ionic and Covalent Compounds Experimentally
periods.section_anchor: 9.6 Properties of the Ionic and the Covalent Compounds
materials: Five compounds: camphor, NaCl, CuSO₄, sugar, naphthalene
Three solvents: water, kerosene, petrol (in small labelled bottles)
Conductivity circuit: 9 V battery, connecting wires, graphite electrodes, small bulb or LED
periods.visual_aids: Board copy of Table 9.2 (blank) for students to fill: rows = compounds, columns = solubility in each solvent and conductivity in solid/solution

time_bands.activity: Teacher sets up the conductivity circuit as a demonstration and shows students how a lit bulb indicates current flow. Groups are assigned their compounds and solvents, and the blank Table 9.2 is distributed or copied from the board.

Groups carry out Activity 9.4 in two parts: first testing solubility of each compound in water, kerosene, and petrol; then testing conductivity in solid form and in aqueous solution using the circuit. All observations are recorded in Table 9.2.

Groups compare tables and sort the five compounds into two categories based on shared behaviour. Students write three pattern statements: one about solubility in water vs. organic solvents, one about conductivity in solid state, one about conductivity in solution.
Teacher previews the explanation to come: the pattern in the data reflects a structural difference — fixed ions in a lattice vs. mobile ions in solution vs. no ions at all.

periods.teacher_notes: Safety precaution: kerosene and petrol are flammable — ensure no open flames and adequate ventilation during the experiment. Students often predict that all dissolved substances will conduct; the sugar-in-water result (dissolves but does not conduct) is the key anomaly to highlight, since it reveals that dissolving and ionising are different processes. Encourage groups to look for exceptions in their own data before writing pattern statements, so the pattern comes from the evidence rather than from prior assumption.

periods.activity_title: Ions in the Lattice, Ions in Solution — Explaining the Property Patterns
periods.section_anchor: 9.6 Properties of the Ionic and the Covalent Compounds
materials: Students' completed Table 9.2 from the previous unit
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram: NaCl crystal lattice (fixed ions, no current) vs NaCl dissolved (free ions, current flows) vs sugar dissolved (no ions, no current)

time_bands.activity: Teacher returns to the pattern statements students wrote during Activity 9.4 and asks: what structural reason explains why NaCl does not conduct as a solid but does conduct in solution, while sugar does neither? Groups discuss before the explanation is given.

Teacher explains the ionic lattice model: ions are held in fixed positions in the solid (no charge carriers can move), but dissolving in water frees the ions to migrate toward electrodes. Contrast with sugar: molecules dissolve but do not produce ions, so no charge carriers exist.

Students apply the model: for each of the five compounds from Activity 9.4, they write a two-sentence structural explanation for its conductivity behaviour — referencing whether ions are present, fixed, or mobile.

Teacher introduces the melting and boiling point comparison: ionic compounds have high melting points (strong inter-ionic attractions must be overcome); covalent compounds generally have low ones. Students link this back to the lattice diagram.

periods.teacher_notes: Having gathered the experimental data in Activity 9.4, this unit provides the structural explanation; resist the urge to give the explanation first — let students struggle briefly with the question in the opening discussion so the model feels like an answer rather than a given. The most important conceptual move is separating 'dissolving' from 'ionising': sugar dissolves completely yet conducts nothing, which is a powerful counter-example to the misconception that all dissolved substances become ions. The melting point contrast closes the loop on why the lattice matters beyond conductivity.

periods.activity_title: Summing Atomic Masses — Calculating Molecular Mass of Covalent Compounds
materials: Periodic table or atomic mass reference card
periods.visual_aids: Board worked calculation for H₂O and CO₂ with each step labelled: formula → identify atoms and count → multiply atomic mass × count → sum

time_bands.activity: Teacher defines molecular mass and explains why it applies only to covalent compounds — ionic compounds form 3-D crystals with no discrete molecules (connecting back to the lattice structure established in the bonding unit). Demonstrates Worked Example 9.4: H₂O = (1 × 2) + (16 × 1) = 18 u.

Teacher demonstrates Worked Example 9.5: CO₂ = (12 × 1) + (16 × 2) = 44 u. Students then calculate molecular mass for HCl, NH₃, and CH₄ independently, writing each step as shown in the worked examples.

Students calculate the molecular mass of two more complex covalent formulae (CCl₄ and C₂H₅OH) and verify their answers with a partner. Teacher circulates to check that students are using the formula to determine how many of each atom are present, not guessing.

Class discussion: teacher asks — would the molecular mass of H₂O change if you used ocean water versus river water? Students connect the answer back to Proust's Law, consolidating the link between fixed composition and fixed molecular mass.

periods.teacher_notes: Students occasionally confuse molecular mass with atomic mass — emphasise that molecular mass is calculated from the formula and accounts for the number of each atom present. The question about ocean water versus river water is deliberately reminiscent of Proust's Law from Section 9.2; the law established that water's composition is always 1:8 by mass, which means molecular mass is always 18 u regardless of source. Ensure students are writing units (u or amu) throughout, as this is frequently omitted.
homework: Calculate the molecular mass of the following covalent compounds, showing all working: (a) H₂SO₄ (use H = 1, S = 32, O = 16), (b) C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose, use C = 12, H = 1, O = 16). State the number of atoms of each element before calculating.

periods.activity_title: Formula Unit Mass — Calculating the Mass of an Ionic Formula Unit
periods.section_anchor: 9.8 Formula Unit Mass of Ionic Compounds
materials: Periodic table or atomic mass reference card
periods.visual_aids: Board worked calculation for Na₂O and Ca(NO₃)₂ with bracket-expansion step clearly shown

time_bands.activity: Teacher contrasts molecular mass (covalent) with formula unit mass (ionic): since NaCl forms a lattice rather than discrete molecules, the relevant mass unit is the simplest whole-number ratio of ions — the formula unit. Explains that the calculation method is the same arithmetic but the concept is different.

Teacher demonstrates Worked Example 9.6: Na₂O = (23 × 2) + (16 × 1) = 62 u. Then demonstrates Worked Example 9.7: Ca(NO₃)₂ — shows the bracket-expansion step: 1 Ca + 2 N + 6 O = 40 + 28 + 96 = 164 u. Students follow along and write each step.

Students calculate the formula unit mass of NaCl, MgO, AlCl₃, and K₂SO₄ independently. They must show the bracket-expansion step where relevant and state the number of each type of atom in the formula unit before calculating.
Peer-check and class debrief. Teacher highlights the most common error — failing to expand brackets for polyatomic ions — by working through K₂SO₄ on the board with student input.

periods.teacher_notes: The key conceptual point is the 'formula unit' as distinct from 'molecule' — ionic compounds do not exist as individual molecules, so calling the result 'molecular mass' is a conceptual error students should learn to avoid. The bracket expansion in Ca(NO₃)₂ is where most arithmetic errors occur; slowing down on this step and explicitly writing '2 × NO₃ means 2 N and 6 O' before calculating prevents most mistakes. Students who correctly handled molecular mass in the previous unit should be able to transfer the arithmetic; the new element is entirely the conceptual framing.
homework: Calculate the formula unit mass of the following ionic compounds, showing all steps including bracket expansion where needed: (a) Al₂(SO₄)₃ (use Al = 27, S = 32, O = 16), (b) Fe(OH)₃ (use Fe = 56, O = 16, H = 1). State the formula unit and the number of atoms of each element.

periods.activity_title: Formulae, Masses, and Bonds — An Integrated Problem-Solving Review
periods.section_anchor: 9.5 Writing Chemical Formulae / 9.7 Molecular Mass of Covalent Compounds / 9.8 Formula Unit Mass of Ionic Compounds
materials: Periodic table or atomic mass reference card
periods.visual_aids: Board decision tree: Is the compound ionic or covalent? → Write formula using criss-cross → Identify formula type → Calculate molecular mass OR formula unit mass

time_bands.activity: Teacher presents the decision tree on the board and walks through one example end-to-end: given 'magnesium nitrate', identify it as ionic, write the formula Mg(NO₃)₂ via criss-cross, then calculate its formula unit mass (148 u).

Students work through a tiered worksheet: Part A — write formulae for six compounds (mix of ionic and covalent) using criss-cross; Part B — classify each as ionic or covalent and state which mass concept applies; Part C — calculate the molecular or formula unit mass for three of the six.

Students swap worksheets for peer review, focusing on Part B classification. Any disagreements are flagged and brought to the class. Teacher leads a brief discussion on borderline cases, reinforcing the electron-sharing vs. electron-transfer criterion.
Students identify which step in the three-step process (write formula → classify → calculate mass) they found most uncertain and write one question about it. Teacher collects the questions.

periods.teacher_notes: The decision tree makes the whole-chapter reasoning chain visible in a single diagram; students who have learned each step in isolation often struggle to sequence them without this scaffold. The most likely sticking point is classification — students may apply criss-cross correctly yet misidentify a compound as ionic when it is covalent or vice versa; the electron-sharing/transfer criterion from Sections 9.4.1 and 9.4.2 is the arbiter. Collect the exit questions genuinely — they will reveal which step most students are uncertain about.

periods.activity_title: Connecting the Chapter — Laws, Bonds, Formulae, and Masses in a Novel Context
periods.section_anchor: 9.1 Law of Conservation of Mass / 9.2 Law of Constant Proportions / 9.3 Dalton's Atomic Theory / 9.4 How Atoms Combine? / 9.4.1 Bonding by sharing of electrons — Covalent Bond / 9.4.2 Bonding by electron transfer — Ionic bond / 9.5 Writing Chemical Formulae / 9.6 Properties of the Ionic and the Covalent Compounds / 9.7 Molecular Mass of Covalent Compounds / 9.8 Formula Unit Mass of Ionic Compounds
materials: Periodic table or atomic mass reference card

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the exit questions collected in the previous unit, addressing the two or three most common uncertainties briefly before moving on — not re-teaching but clarifying the sharpest sticking points.

Groups receive a scenario card describing an unfamiliar compound (e.g. 'Compound X contains aluminium and sulfur. It forms crystals, dissolves in water, and its solution conducts electricity. Aluminium has a valency of 3, sulfur a valency of 2.'). Groups must: identify the bond type, write the formula using criss-cross, name the compound, calculate its formula unit mass, and predict one more property from Section 9.6.

Groups present their reasoning (not just answers) to the class. Peers question the reasoning — e.g. 'Why did you choose formula unit mass rather than molecular mass?' Teacher facilitates without correcting until all groups have spoken.

Teacher draws the chapter's conceptual arc on the board: from empirical laws (conservation of mass, constant proportions) → atomic theory → bonding mechanisms → formulae → properties → masses. Students annotate their own copy, linking each section to the one piece of evidence or rule that anchors it.

periods.teacher_notes: The scenario card task is deliberately novel — students cannot recall the answer; they must reason from the chapter's tools. The most likely error is students writing molecular mass for an ionic compound; asking 'does this substance form discrete molecules?' during the presentation phase surfaces this misconception cleanly. The closing arc diagram is the chapter's synthesis moment — ensure every student leaves with a completed annotated arc in their notebook, as it consolidates the logical spine that runs from Lavoisier's law all the way to formula unit mass.

questions.question_text: In Activity 9.2, when vinegar reacted with baking soda in Set-up 1 (balloon beside flask, open system), the final mass reading was lower than the initial reading. Which statement best explains this observation?

options.label: A
options.text: Carbon dioxide gas produced in the reaction escaped the system, so the measured mass of the remaining substances was lower.

options.label: B
options.text: Mass is not conserved in chemical reactions involving gases, only in reactions that produce solids.

options.label: C
options.text: Some of the vinegar evaporated during the reaction, reducing the total mass.

options.label: D
options.text: The baking soda was not fully used up, so some mass was unaccounted for in the final reading.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses evaporation with gas production — the student attributes the mass loss to the solvent rather than to the gaseous product of the chemical reaction.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Holds the misconception that the Law of Conservation of Mass does not apply to reactions producing gases, rather than understanding that the law applies to closed systems capturing all products.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Attributes the mass discrepancy to incomplete reaction rather than to escaped product — confuses reaction completion with system closure.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who struggle with abstract gas concepts can be asked to recall the balloon-as-capture-device set-up and reason about what the balloon was designed to prevent. Students who answer quickly can be asked to explain what result Set-up 2 gave and why it differed.

questions.question_text: Sodium chloride always contains sodium and chlorine in a mass ratio of 23 : 35.5. A student is given 46 g of sodium and told to prepare the maximum possible quantity of sodium chloride. (a) Calculate the mass of chlorine that will react with all 46 g of sodium. (b) Calculate the total mass of sodium chloride formed. (c) If the student had used only 23 g of sodium, what mass of chlorine would be needed and what mass of sodium chloride would form?
expected_elements: Recognises that sodium and chlorine combine in the fixed ratio 23 : 35.5 regardless of the quantity of compound prepared.
Part (a): scales the ratio — 46 g Na is twice 23 g, so chlorine required = 2 × 35.5 = 71 g.
Part (b): total mass of NaCl = 46 + 71 = 117 g (or applies Law of Conservation of Mass).
Part (c): 23 g Na → 35.5 g Cl → 58.5 g NaCl; recognises the ratio is proportional.
Explicit reference to the Law of Constant Proportions as the basis for using the same ratio in both parts.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the two-part scaling difficult can be encouraged to write the ratio as a fraction (35.5/23) and multiply by the given mass of sodium. Students who complete parts (a) and (b) quickly can be asked to explain why the ratio does not change even when the quantity of sodium is halved.

questions.question_text: The Law of Conservation of Mass and the Law of Constant Proportions were established experimentally before Dalton proposed his atomic theory in 1808. Explain how specific postulates of Dalton's atomic theory account for each of these two laws. In your answer, identify the relevant postulate(s) for each law and explain the logical connection — why the postulate makes the experimental law inevitable rather than coincidental.
look_for: Correctly identifies the postulate that atoms are indivisible and cannot be created or destroyed as the basis for conservation of mass, and explains why atomic rearrangement (not creation/destruction) produces the same total mass.

Correctly identifies the postulates that atoms of a given element are identical and that atoms combine in fixed whole-number ratios as the basis for constant proportions, explaining why identical atoms always deliver the same mass ratio.

Makes the logical connection explicit — not just 'postulate X explains law Y' but 'because atoms are identical and combine in fixed ratios, the mass fraction of each element in a compound cannot vary from sample to sample'.
Uses concrete examples from the chapter (e.g. hydrogen and oxygen forming water, magnesium burning in air) to anchor the abstract reasoning.
Avoids restating the laws and postulates without connecting them — the analytical move is the explanation of why the postulate makes the law necessary.

ECR.inclusivity: Students who struggle to begin can be asked to address one law at a time and identify just one postulate for each before writing. Students who produce a strong response can be extended by asking whether any postulate of Dalton's theory was later shown to be incomplete or incorrect, and what evidence challenged it.

questions.question_text: An atom has 6 electrons in its valence shell. Based on the octet rule, which prediction about this atom's bonding behaviour is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The atom is already stable and will not form any chemical bonds.

options.label: B
options.text: The atom needs 2 more electrons to complete its octet, so it is likely to gain or share electrons rather than donate them.

options.label: C
options.text: The atom will donate its 6 valence electrons to another atom to achieve stability.

options.label: D
options.text: The atom will share exactly 6 electron pairs with neighbouring atoms to reach stability.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Applies the donation strategy to an atom with more than four valence electrons — confuses the 'fewer than four donate' rule with 'more than four donate', reversing the principle.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Treats any electron count other than 8 as already stable, misapplying the noble-gas criterion — possibly confusing this atom with helium (2) or a full octet (8).
what_each_option_reveals.D: Confuses the number of valence electrons with the number of electron pairs shared — the atom needs 2 more electrons (2 bonds), not 6 electron pairs.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain can be directed to count how many electrons the atom needs to reach 8 before predicting the strategy. Students who answer confidently can be asked to name a real element with 6 valence electrons and identify whether it forms covalent or ionic bonds in practice.

questions.question_text: (a) Draw the electron-dot diagram for Cl₂, showing all valence electrons. Identify the type of covalent bond formed and explain why two chlorine atoms form exactly one bond rather than two. (b) Apply the prefix naming system to write the systematic names of the following covalent compounds: (i) N₂O₄, (ii) SF₆, (iii) CS₂. (c) H₂O has a common name. Write it and explain why it is used instead of the systematic name.
expected_elements: Part (a): electron-dot diagram showing each Cl with 7 valence electrons; one pair of electrons shared between the two atoms; six lone-pair electrons on each Cl after sharing; identifies the bond as a single covalent bond.

Part (a) explanation: each chlorine atom has 7 valence electrons and needs 1 more to reach 8; sharing one electron pair provides that one electron, completing the octet for both — a second bond would give each atom 9 electrons, exceeding the octet.
Part (b)(i): N₂O₄ — dinitrogen tetroxide (vowel-dropping rule: 'a' dropped before 'o').
Part (b)(ii): SF₆ — sulfur hexafluoride.
Part (b)(iii): CS₂ — carbon disulfide.
Part (c): common name is 'water'; it is used because it predates the systematic naming convention and is universally understood — systematic names apply to compounds without established common names.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who find the electron-dot diagram difficult can be prompted to first write out the electron configuration of chlorine (2,8,7) and then count how many electrons are in the outermost shell. Students who complete all parts can be asked to draw the electron-dot diagram for O₂ and explain why it forms a double bond while Cl₂ forms a single bond.

questions.question_text: Magnesium (atomic number 12) and oxygen (atomic number 8) react to form magnesium oxide. (a) State the number of valence electrons in each atom and predict which atom will donate electrons and which will accept them. (b) Show the electron transfer step by step: state how many electrons are transferred, write the resulting ions with their charges, and give the proton and electron counts for each ion. (c) Name the type of bond formed and the compound produced.
expected_elements: Part (a): Mg has 2 valence electrons (electron configuration 2,8,2); O has 6 valence electrons (2,6). Mg donates (fewer than 4 valence electrons); O accepts (more than 4).

Part (b): Mg transfers 2 electrons to O. Mg becomes Mg²⁺ (12 protons, 10 electrons). O becomes O²⁻ (8 protons, 10 electrons). Both ions now have 8 electrons in their outermost shell, satisfying the octet rule.
Part (c): the bond formed is an ionic bond (electrostatic attraction between Mg²⁺ and O²⁻); the compound is magnesium oxide (cation name first, anion name ends in -ide).

SCR.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about which atom donates can be prompted to write the full electron configuration for each atom and count the outermost shell electrons before deciding. Students who complete all parts correctly can be asked to compare this to the NaCl example and identify one structural similarity and one difference between MgO and NaCl.

questions.question_text: Using the criss-cross method, write the chemical formulae for the following compounds. Show all working steps: symbol, valency/charge written below, criss-cross, and simplification where needed. (a) Aluminium oxide (Al³⁺, O²⁻). (b) Calcium nitrate (Ca²⁺, NO₃⁻). (c) Zinc hydroxide (Zn²⁺, OH⁻). For (b) and (c), state the rule that requires brackets in the formula.
expected_elements: Part (a): Al valency 3, O valency 2; criss-cross gives Al₂O₃; no simplification needed (2 and 3 share no common factor); correct formula Al₂O₃.

Part (b): Ca charge 2, NO₃ charge 1; criss-cross gives Ca₁(NO₃)₂; subscript 1 not written; correct formula Ca(NO₃)₂. Bracket rule: NO₃ is a polyatomic ion that appears more than once, so brackets are used.
Part (c): Zn charge 2, OH charge 1; criss-cross gives Zn₁(OH)₂; subscript 1 not written; correct formula Zn(OH)₂. Bracket rule: OH is a polyatomic ion appearing more than once.
Charges are NOT written in the final formula for any compound.
Division/simplification step is shown for (a) even if no common factor exists — student must demonstrate awareness of the check.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about when to use brackets can be asked to first check whether the anion is a single element or a group of elements — groups appearing more than once always require brackets. Students who complete all three parts correctly can be asked to write the formula for iron(III) sulfate (Fe³⁺, SO₄²⁻) and explain why brackets are needed there too.

questions.visual_stimulus:
Substance | Solid state conducts? | Dissolved in water conducts? | Soluble in water? | Soluble in kerosene?
NaCl | No | Yes | Yes | No
Sugar | No | No | Yes | No
Naphthalene | No | No | No | Yes
CuSO₄ | No | Yes | Yes | No
Camphor | No | No | No | Yes
questions.task: Refer to the table of observations from the conductivity and solubility investigation. (a) Group the five substances into ionic compounds and covalent compounds based on the data. Justify each grouping using at least two columns of data. (b) NaCl does not conduct electricity in the solid state but does conduct when dissolved in water. Using the ionic lattice model, explain this difference in behaviour. (c) Sugar also dissolves in water but does not conduct in solution. Explain why sugar's behaviour in solution differs from that of NaCl, even though both dissolve completely.
questions.scaffold: For part (a), look at which substances conduct when dissolved — this is your strongest sorting criterion, but check it against solubility in kerosene as a second piece of evidence. For part (b), think about what happens to the ions in the lattice when water is added. For part (c), ask: does dissolving always produce ions?
format_of_output: Written grouping with justification for part (a)
Explanatory paragraph for part (b) referencing the lattice model
Comparative explanation for part (c) distinguishing dissolving from ionising

OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The section's implied_lo requires students to reason from evidence about ion mobility and arrangement; the data table from Activity 9.4 provides exactly the empirical observations that demand a structural explanation, making data interpretation the most natural vehicle.
OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: Students demonstrate that they can read experimental data to classify compounds and then apply the ionic lattice model to explain the pattern — moving from observation to structural reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold directs students to conductivity-in-solution as the primary sort criterion and kerosene solubility as confirmation; it prompts the lattice thinking for part (b) and the dissolving-vs-ionising distinction for part (c). Strong responses will go beyond the scaffold prompts to offer independent reasoning.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: groups all five correctly with two independent data-based justifications; explains lattice → fixed ions → no current, and water → free ions → current in part (b); explicitly distinguishes dissolving (physical separation of molecules) from ionising (producing charge carriers) in part (c). Weak: groups correctly but without citing specific columns; describes NaCl dissolving without mentioning ion mobility; treats sugar's non-conductance as anomalous rather than explicable.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find part (c) challenging can be asked to describe what is in the NaCl solution (Na⁺ and Cl⁻ ions) and then describe what is in the sugar solution (sugar molecules) before comparing. Students who complete all parts fluently can be asked to predict the conductivity behaviour of molten NaCl and justify their prediction using the same lattice model.

questions.question_text: The molecular mass of ammonia (NH₃) is calculated using the atomic masses N = 14 u and H = 1 u. Which of the following correctly gives the molecular mass of NH₃ and identifies the type of compound to which 'molecular mass' applies?

options.label: A
options.text: Molecular mass = 15 u; molecular mass applies only to ionic compounds because they form lattice structures.

options.label: B
options.text: Molecular mass = 17 u; molecular mass applies only to covalent compounds because ionic compounds form 3-D crystal lattices, not discrete molecules.

options.label: C
options.text: Molecular mass = 17 u; molecular mass applies to both covalent and ionic compounds.

options.label: D
options.text: Molecular mass = 42 u; molecular mass applies only to covalent compounds.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Calculates correctly (17 u) but misapplies 'molecular mass' to ionic compounds — does not connect the term to the presence of discrete molecules, which ionic lattice structures lack.
what_each_option_reveals.A: Miscalculates by counting only one hydrogen atom (14 + 1 = 15) and reverses the applicability rule — confuses the lattice property of ionic compounds with the meaning of molecular mass.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Multiplies all atomic masses together or adds them incorrectly (perhaps 14 × 3 = 42), and while correctly restricting molecular mass to covalent compounds, reveals a fundamental arithmetic error in the calculation.

MCQ.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about the calculation can be directed to write out every atom present (N, H, H, H) and add the atomic mass for each one individually before summing. Students who answer correctly quickly can be asked to explain why the molecular mass of water is always 18 u regardless of the water's source, connecting back to Proust's Law.

questions.question_text: Calculate the formula unit mass of aluminium sulfate, Al₂(SO₄)₃. Use the atomic masses: Al = 27 u, S = 32 u, O = 16 u. Show all working steps, including the bracket-expansion step, and explain why this compound requires 'formula unit mass' rather than 'molecular mass'.
expected_elements: States the number of each type of atom: 2 Al, 3 S, 12 O (from expanding (SO₄)₃ → 3 S and 3 × 4 O = 12 O).
Bracket expansion step explicitly written: (SO₄)₃ means 3 sulfur atoms and 12 oxygen atoms.
Correct final answer: 342 u.

Explanation: Al₂(SO₄)₃ is an ionic compound; its ions arrange in a 3-D crystal lattice rather than forming discrete molecules, so 'molecular mass' does not apply — 'formula unit mass' refers to the mass of the simplest whole-number ratio of ions in the formula.

SCR.inclusivity: Students who are uncertain about bracket expansion can be encouraged to first rewrite the formula with the bracket fully expanded (2 Al + 3 S + 12 O) before doing any arithmetic. Students who complete the calculation correctly can be asked to compare this to the formula unit mass of Na₂O (62 u) and explain which compound has a larger formula unit mass and why.
